Giovanni Gabrieli. A Venetian master who lived around 1557 to 1612 and fundamentally reshaped what ensemble music could express through his spatial and architectural approach to composition. He exploited St. Mark's multiple organ lofts and choir galleries to create immersive acoustic effects.

Gabrieli pioneered polychoral composition by dividing singers or instruments into multiple spatial groups that would echo and answer one another. This technique transformed how music could fill a physical space. He composed over one hundred fifty works, with In Ecclesiis standing as a masterpiece of antiphonal dialogue that combines voices and instruments in layered, coloristic grandeur. For the last twelve years of his life, he served as maestro di cappella at St. Mark's Basilica in Venice, following his uncle Andrea Gabrieli.

Beyond vocal music, he wrote virtuoso instrumental works including canzonas and sonatas for various ensembles, exploiting the rising status of instrumental music in the early Baroque. He excelled in both sacred and secular vocal music, blending rich counterpoint with harmonic color and dramatic dynamic contrast. What set him apart was his use of dynamic markings, writing forte and piano explicitly into his scores, along with specific tempo indications. This systematic approach to performance instruction was unusually precise for his era and indicated a move toward modern Baroque performance practice. His work laid the foundation for how composers would think about sound as something that could be shaped by the space itself.
